hex.label: The file's bytes. Move the selection with the arrow keys, hold Shift to mark a range.
hex.noRegion: This part of the file belongs to no recognised block.
hex.unknownStructure: Conbert doesn't know this format's structure (yet) – you see the raw bytes. Explained are PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, ICO, TIFF, WAV, WebP, AVI, MP3, FLAC, OGG, MP4/MOV, HEIC, AVIF, PDF, ZIP (also DOCX, XLSX, EPUB …), GZIP and TAR.
hex.moreRegions: The file has more blocks – only the first ones are listed here.
hex.inspectorHelp: The same bytes from the selected position, read in different ways. Bigger numbers are made of several bytes: a 4-byte number uses the clicked byte and the three after it. That's why the values change although two clicked bytes are the same (e.g. 00) – their neighbours differ. Little endian (LE) means: the smallest byte first – that's how Intel computers and most formats store numbers. Big endian (BE) is the other way round. Which reading is right depends on the format.
hex.searchNone: Nothing found – not further on (or back) either.
hex.searchInvalid: Please enter bytes as hexadecimal numbers, e.g. “89 50 4E 47”.
hex.minimap: The whole file at a glance – click to jump there.
hex.inspectorReads: Read from {{offset}} – the clicked byte and the ones after it (up to {{count}}):

hashes.algorithmsHelp: SHA-256 is today's standard and listed on most download pages. MD5 and SHA-1 are old: they are fine for spotting transfer errors but don't protect against deliberate tampering. CRC32 is very short and used inside ZIP files, for example. BLAKE3 is modern and especially fast.
hashes.bigFile: The file is {{size}} – start the calculation when you need it.
hashes.failed: The checksums couldn't be computed. Please choose the file again.
hashes.compareHelp: Paste the checksum given e.g. on the download page. Conbert tells the method from its length – spaces, colons or a file name behind it are fine.
hashes.match: It fits! The file is unchanged, bit for bit ({{algorithm}}).
hashes.different: It doesn't fit ({{algorithm}}). The file is a different one, was changed or got damaged while downloading. Best download it again.
hashes.notComputed: That looks like {{algorithm}} – switch the method on above and compute again.
hashes.invalid: That doesn't look like a checksum. Hexadecimal characters (0–9, a–f) are expected.

entropy.failed: The file couldn't be read. Please choose it again.
entropy.empty: The file is empty – nothing to measure here.

levels.uniform: Very uniform: almost always the same bytes, e.g. empty areas or single-colour surfaces. Compresses extremely well.
levels.structured: Structured: some bytes are much more common than others – typical for text, tables and programs. Compresses well.
levels.dense: Dense: fairly mixed data, e.g. uncompressed picture data or audio. Compression still helps a bit.
levels.random: Almost random: this is what compressed (JPG, MP4, ZIP) or encrypted data looks like. Compressing again gains practically nothing.

entropy.chartLabel: Entropy across the file, {{value}} bits per byte on average
entropy.clickHint: Click into the chart to see that spot in the hex view.
entropy.sampled: The file is big: only the start of each section was measured. The picture is still accurate.
entropy.why: Compressing means writing repetitions and common patterns more briefly. Data with high entropy has no such patterns left – every byte is as surprising as a dice roll. That's why a ZIP full of JPG photos is hardly smaller than the photos themselves.

structure.appended: Data behind the actual end of the file ({{bytes}}). Programs reading the format simply overlook it.
structure.appendedKnown: “{{format}}” ({{bytes}}) behind the actual end of the file. That's how the “archive in a picture” trick works.

png.signature: PNG mark: 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A. The line breaks in it reveal whether the file was mangled in transfer.
png.crc: Checksum (CRC32) of the block – lets a program notice a damaged block.

chunks.IHDR: Picture header: {{width}} × {{height}} pixels, plus colour depth and colour type.
chunks.PLTE: Colour palette – for pictures with at most 256 colours.
chunks.IDAT: Picture data, compressed (like in a ZIP).
chunks.IEND: End of the picture. Whatever follows is no longer part of the PNG.
chunks.tEXt: Text note, e.g. program or author.
chunks.iTXt: Text note with special characters, often XMP metadata.
chunks.gAMA: Gamma value: how bright the colours are meant to be.
chunks.cHRM: Exact position of the primary colours.
chunks.sRGB: The picture uses the standard sRGB colour space.
chunks.tIME: When the picture was last changed.
chunks.eXIf: EXIF metadata (camera, date, maybe GPS location).
chunks.acTL: Animated PNG: number of frames and repeats.
chunks.fcTL: Animated PNG: size and duration of a frame.
chunks.fdAT: Animated PNG: data of a frame.
chunks.other: An additional block Conbert doesn't know in detail.
chunks.ziPp: The “ziPp” block is a clever trick: it is not a standard PNG building block, but smuggles the ZIP archive into the picture structure as an extra block that viewers ignore.

jpg.soi: JPEG start (FF D8): the picture begins here.
jpg.eoi: JPEG end (FF D9). Whatever follows is no longer part of the picture.
jpg.scan: The actual picture data, heavily compressed.

markers.app0: JFIF header: version and pixel density.
markers.exif: EXIF metadata: camera, date, exposure, maybe GPS location and a small preview.
markers.xmp: XMP metadata, e.g. from Lightroom or Photoshop.
markers.dht: Huffman table: the key the picture data is packed with.
markers.dqt: Quantisation table: sets the JPEG quality. This decides how much detail is lost.
markers.dri: Distance of the restart points in the picture data.
markers.sofProgressive: Picture header (progressive – loads blurry first, then sharp): {{width}} × {{height}} pixels.

gif.signature: GIF mark with version (GIF87a or GIF89a).
gif.palette: Colour palette with {{colors}} colours – GIF can do at most 256.
gif.trailer: GIF end (3B). Whatever follows is no longer part of the picture.
gif.gce: Control block: display time and transparency of the next frame.
gif.app: Program block, usually “NETSCAPE2.0” for the endless loop.

bmp.fileHeader: File header: size ({{bytes}}) and where the pixels start.
bmp.pixels: The pixels, uncompressed – that's why BMP files are so big.

riff.header: RIFF header: total size and kind of file (WAVE, WEBP or AVI).

chunks.fmt: Sound format: sample rate, channels, bits per sample.
chunks.list: List with extra info, e.g. title or artist.
chunks.vp8x: Extended WebP header: size, transparency, animation.
chunks.anmf: A frame of a WebP animation.
chunks.avih: AVI header: frame rate and size.

pdf.body: Content: pages, fonts, pictures – as numbered objects.
pdf.trailer: PDF end: pointer to the table of contents and the %%EOF mark.

zip.prefix: Data in front of the actual archive ({{bytes}}). ZIP programs skip it.
zip.prefixKnown: In front of the archive sits “{{format}}” ({{bytes}}). That's why the file is two things at once – ZIP reads its table of contents from the end.
zip.local: Entry header: name, date and compression of a file in the archive.
zip.dataEncrypted: Content of the file, encrypted ({{bytes}} unpacked).
zip.descriptor: Checksum and size of the entry, given afterwards.
zip.central: Table of contents: list of all {{count}} entries with their positions.
zip.zip64: ZIP64 addition for very large archives.
zip.end: End of the archive: says where the table of contents starts.

bmff.media: The actual video, sound or picture data (mdat).

boxes.ftyp: File type: which variant (MP4, MOV, HEIC, AVIF …) and what it is compatible with.
boxes.moov: Movie description: duration, tracks, where each frame lies.
boxes.mvhd: Movie header: duration and time scale.
boxes.tkhd: Track header: size and duration of the track.
boxes.mdhd: Media header: time scale and language.
boxes.stbl: Table of where each frame lies.
boxes.stsd: Codec of the track (e.g. H.264, AAC).
boxes.co64: Where the data blocks lie (big files).
boxes.stss: Key frames – you can jump to these.
boxes.elst: Edit list: which part is shown.
boxes.pitm: Which picture is the main one.
boxes.iloc: Where the pictures lie in the file.
boxes.idat: Small picture data right in the metadata.

mp3.id3: ID3 tag: title, artist, album, cover.
mp3.padding: Filler bytes in the tag – room for later changes.
mp3.frameHeader: Header of the first sound piece: bitrate, sample rate, channels.
mp3.audio: The sound data, compressed piece by piece.
mp3.id3v1: Old ID3v1 tag at the end of the file (128 bytes).

blocks.streaminfo: Sound details: sample rate, channels, bits, length.
blocks.padding: Filler bytes – room for later tags.

ogg.page: OGG page: a piece of the file with its own checksum.
ogg.data: Content of the page (sound or header data).

tiff.header: TIFF header: byte order and where the first directory lies.
tiff.ifd: Directory with {{count}} entries: size, colours, camera, where the picture data lies.

gz.header: GZIP header: packing method, date, original name.
gz.trailer: Checksum and size of the unpacked data.

tar.header: Entry header (512 bytes): name, size, date, permissions.
tar.data: Content of the file ({{bytes}}), padded to full 512 bytes.
tar.end: End of the archive: two empty blocks.

ico.header: ICO header: kind and number of pictures.
ico.entry: Directory entry: size and position of a picture.
ico.png: An icon picture in PNG format.
ico.bitmap: An icon picture as a bitmap.

mkv.signature: EBML signature – MKV and WebM files start like this.
mkv.header: EBML header: which kind of file (matroska or webm) and which version.
mkv.segment: Start of the segment: everything else lies inside it – description, tracks and the actual data.

elements.seekHead: Table of contents: where in the segment the description, tracks and seek points are.
elements.info: General details: duration, title and which program made the file.
elements.tracks: The tracks: which video, sound and subtitle tracks there are and which codec packed them.
elements.cluster: A piece of the film: video and sound data for a few seconds.
elements.attachments: Attached files, e.g. fonts for subtitles or a cover.
elements.chapters: Chapters with names and start times.
elements.void: Placeholder – empty space for later changes.

detective.failed: The file couldn't be searched. Please choose it again.
detective.encryptedHint: Entries with a lock symbol are encrypted. Enter the password above to download them one by one, or open the whole archive with 7-Zip.
detective.zeroWidthHint: These characters are invisible in any editor but can carry a secret message or mark a copied text. The “invisible text” trick to decode them is coming soon.
detective.truncated: There are more finds – only the first 200 are listed.

findings.appended: {{bytes}} of unknown data hang behind the end of the file.
findings.appendedKnown: Hidden behind the end of the file: “{{format}}” ({{bytes}}).
findings.appendedPadding: {{bytes}} of filler bytes behind the end of the file – usually harmless, some cameras and programs do that.
findings.motionPhoto: Moving photo: a short video ({{bytes}}) sits behind the picture – that's how many phones store “Live” or “Motion” photos.
findings.prefix: {{bytes}} of other data sit in front of the archive.
findings.prefixKnown: In front of the archive sits “{{format}}” ({{bytes}}) – the file is two things at once.
findings.embedded: In the middle of the file sits “{{format}}” ({{bytes}}).
findings.thumbnail: Preview picture in the EXIF data ({{bytes}}). Careful: it sometimes still shows what you cropped away later.
findings.pdfObject: Embedded “{{format}}” in the PDF ({{bytes}}) – usually a normal picture on a page.
findings.zeroWidth: {{count}} invisible characters found in the text.
findings.zeroWidthMessage: The text holds a message made of invisible characters ({{count}} characters) – written with Conbert.
findings.zeroWidthMessageLocked: The text holds a password-protected message made of invisible characters ({{count}} characters) – written with Conbert.
findings.stegoPicture: The pixels hold a Conbert message ({{bytes}} packed).
findings.stegoPictureLocked: The pixels hold a password-protected Conbert message ({{bytes}}).
findings.stegoAudio: The samples hold a Conbert message ({{bytes}} packed).
findings.stegoAudioLocked: The samples hold a password-protected Conbert message ({{bytes}}).
findings.lsbSuspicious: The lowest bits of the colour values look random in the top {{percent}} % of the picture – a typical sign of hidden data.
findings.sealedMeta: A password-protected secret message sits in the metadata here (“CNBZ1:…”).

detective.trickHint: Open the file there again to read the message.
detective.lsbHint: This is a hint, not proof: very noisy photos can look similar. It isn't a Conbert message – the scan would have recognised that directly. Under “Steganography” you can view the lowest bits as a picture.
detective.needsPassword: Please enter the password first to download this file.

errors.encrypted: This file is encrypted with a password. Download the whole archive and open it with 7-Zip or WinRAR.
errors.unsupported-method: This file is packed with a method Conbert can't unpack. Download the whole archive and open it with 7-Zip.
errors.broken: The hidden data is damaged or incomplete and can't be read.
errors.too-big: The file is too big to unpack in the browser. Download the whole archive.
errors.empty: You have not chosen any files to hide yet. Please add some first.
errors.executable: Safety lock: “{{name}}” is a program or script. For safety reasons this is not allowed here, please remove the file.
errors.wrong-password: Sorry, the password is wrong. Please check what you typed.
errors.not-cover: Sorry, this file does not work for the trick. Please choose another one.
errors.not-archive: That is not an archive format I can read. It has to be ZIP, RAR or 7Z.
errors.unchecked: Conbert cannot look inside the archive because the file names are encrypted. Pack the files with “Pack single files” instead.
errors.locked-pdf: This PDF is password-protected. Please remove the protection before you use it.

fields.directorySize: Size of the table of contents
fields.directoryOffset: Table of contents starts at byte

privacy.failed: This file's metadata couldn't be read.
privacy.clean: Nothing notable found – the file's metadata gives away no personal info.
privacy.thumbDiffers: Careful: the preview differs from the picture! The photo was probably cropped or edited – the preview often still shows the old state, including what was cropped away.
privacy.cannotRemove: Conbert can't remove the metadata of this format itself. Convert the file (e.g. to PNG or WebP) – most metadata stays behind.
privacy.officeHowTo: How to remove this in Office: Word, Excel or PowerPoint → File → Info → “Check for Issues” → “Inspect Document”. In LibreOffice: Tools → Options → Security → “Remove personal information on saving”. Accept or delete comments and changes first.

location.title: Where it was taken
location.help: The photo was taken here – often accurate to a few metres. For photos taken at home this gives away your address.

serial.title: Device serial number
serial.help: Lets anyone link all photos of the same camera – even across different accounts.

personTags.title: Tagged people
personTags.help: Names of people tagged on the picture in a program (e.g. Lightroom, Google Photos).

people.title: Names
people.help: Who created or edited the picture or document.

comments.title: Comments and descriptions
comments.help: Text stored in the file – sometimes more than one meant to share.

history.title: Editing history
history.help: Which programs opened and saved the file, sometimes with dates.

software.title: Program
software.help: Which program created or edited the file.

dates.title: Time
dates.help: When the photo was taken or the file created.

thumbnail.title: Hidden preview picture
thumbnail.help: A small picture in the metadata. Programs don't always update it when editing – then it still shows the original.

officeAuthors.title: Authors
officeAuthors.help: Who created the document and saved it last.

officeCompany.title: Company
officeCompany.help: Company or organisation name from the document properties.

officeComments.help: Comments in the document – with the names of whoever wrote them.

officeChanges.help: Deleted and inserted text is still in the document – anyone can make it visible again.

officeHidden.help: Hidden text or hidden sheets – invisible, but still in the file.

officeNotes.help: Notes for the talk – whoever gets the file can read them.

repair.cutAppended: Cut off data behind the end of the file
repair.cutAppendedHelp: Some files carry data behind their actual end – leftovers of programs, or a deliberately hidden archive. Switch this off to keep the hidden data.
repair.nothing: Nothing broken found. If the file still doesn't open, have a look in the file X-ray – maybe it's another format.

pngCrc.help: Every block of a PNG has a checksum. If it doesn't fit, some programs refuse to open the picture. The data itself may still be slightly damaged.

pngCut.title: Removed {{size}} of incomplete data
pngCut.help: The last block was cut off (e.g. an interrupted download) and was removed.

pngEnd.title: Added the missing end of the picture
pngEnd.help: The PNG lacked its closing mark “IEND”. Now every program opens it – the missing lower part stays empty.

jpgEnd.title: Added the missing end of the picture
jpgEnd.help: The JPEG lacked its closing mark (FF D9). Now every program opens it – the missing lower part stays grey.

gifEnd.title: Added the missing end of the GIF
gifEnd.help: The GIF lacked its closing mark. An animation now shows all complete frames.

appended.title: Cut off {{size}} of data behind the end
appended.help: There was data behind the actual end of the file. To keep it, switch the option above off.

extension.title: Extension fixed: “{{name}}”
extension.help: The content didn't fit the extension. With the right one your computer opens the file with the matching program.

pngShortened.title: Saved the cut-off picture data
pngShortened.help: The last block of picture data was cut off (e.g. an interrupted download). Conbert kept what's there and shortened the block to fit – the missing part of the picture stays empty.

ela.notJpeg: This isn't a JPEG. The analysis works best with JPEG photos – for PNG and other formats the result means little.
ela.qualityHelp: Conbert saves the picture with this JPEG quality for the comparison. Best pick about the quality the photo was originally saved with (often 85–95 %). Feel free to try several values.
ela.amplifyHelp: How strongly the differences are brightened. Higher = small differences become visible too.
ela.failed: The picture couldn't be analysed. Is it a picture your browser can show (JPEG, PNG, WebP)?
ela.resultAlt: Error level analysis: bright spots changed more when saved again
ela.read1: An unedited photo is noisy in a similar way everywhere: evenly dark with bright edges and fine patterns.
ela.read2: Suspicious is a clearly bounded area that is much brighter (or darker) than similar areas next to it – like an inserted face or text that glows differently from the rest.
ela.limits: No proof: edges, text and strong colours always glow brighter. If the whole picture was saved again or scaled down after editing (e.g. by messengers), the traces often disappear. Use it as a hint, not a verdict.

treasure.what: What do you want to split?
treasure.secretPlaceholder: e.g. the master password of your password manager
treasure.fileLimit: Up to {{size}} – enough for keys, password lists and notes. Each part is as big as the file.
treasure.totalHelp: How many parts the secret is split into (2 to 16). Each part goes to a different place or person.
treasure.neededHelp: How many parts you need at least to get the secret back. With fewer, nothing at all can be learnt about it.
treasure.neededEffect: Higher = safer, because more people have to help each other, but you may lose fewer parts. Lower = more convenient. 3 of 5 is popular.
treasure.summary: {{total}} parts – any {{needed}} of them bring the secret back. Up to {{lose}} may get lost, and whoever gets hold of only {{leak}} learns nothing.
treasure.handOut: Hand out the parts to different places or people. Don't keep them all together – that would undo the protection. Putting it together takes {{needed}} of them. Conbert keeps nothing: download or copy the parts now.
treasure.partNote: Part of a Conbert treasure map. With {{needed}} such parts the secret can be restored in Conbert under Workshop → Treasure map → Put together.
treasure.saveAll: Download all parts as a ZIP
treasure.paste: Paste parts here (or load them as files)
treasure.noneFound: No parts found yet. A part starts with “conbert-teil:”.

errors.too-few: These are still too few parts. Add more – how many are needed is shown above.
errors.mixed: These parts don't belong to the same treasure map. Check whether a part of another secret has sneaked in.
errors.damaged: A part is damaged – probably a character went missing while copying, or there's a typo. Copy the part again completely.
errors.duplicate: One part is in there twice. Each part only counts once – add a different one.
errors.not-a-share: That doesn't look like a part of a treasure map. A part starts with “conbert-teil:”.
errors.too-big: The secret is too big. Up to {{size}} is allowed. For big files, better use the key vault and split only the password.
errors.bad-count: That number doesn't work: there must be at least 2 parts, at most {{max}}, and you can't require more parts than there are.
errors.unknown: That didn't work. Please try again.

ciphers.shiftHelp: How many places each letter moves along the alphabet. With 3, A becomes D and B becomes E. Caesar himself is said to have used 3.
ciphers.keyHelp: Each letter of the key word says how far the next letter is shifted (A = 0, B = 1 …). Then the word starts over. The longer the word, the harder to crack.
ciphers.notSafe: A computer cracks these scripts in seconds. For real secrets use the key vault – it encrypts with modern cryptography.

caesar.name: Caesar
caesar.help: Every letter moves the same number of places along the alphabet. Umlauts, digits and punctuation stay as they are.
caesar.crack: There are only 25 possible shifts – you simply try them all. Conbert does that for you and sorts the results by how much they look like real English or German text (measured by how often each letter appears: E is the most common one).

rot13.name: ROT13
rot13.help: Caesar with shift 13. Because the alphabet has 26 letters, applying ROT13 twice gives the text back – encrypting and decrypting are the same. Popular online for hiding spoilers.
rot13.crack: No need – anyone who knows ROT13 just applies it once more. It's only meant to stop you from reading something by accident.

atbash.name: Atbash
atbash.help: The alphabet is mirrored: A becomes Z, B becomes Y, C becomes X. One of the oldest known ciphers, found in the Hebrew Bible. Applied twice it gives the text back.
atbash.crack: There is no key – anyone who knows the method can read it right away. Counting letters gives it away quickly too: the most common sign is V, the mirrored E.

vigenere.name: Vigenère
vigenere.help: Like Caesar, but every letter is shifted by a different number – in turn from the key word. It was thought to be “unbreakable” for 300 years.
vigenere.crack: First you guess the length of the key word. Take every 6th letter – with the right length they are all shifted by the same letter, so they behave like normal text in which letters repeat noticeably often. Then you crack each of these columns like Caesar. With short texts one letter of the key can be off.

morse.name: Morse
morse.help: Every character becomes short (·) and long (−) signals – for radio, light or knocking. Words are separated by “/”. Press “Play” to hear it.
morse.crack: Morse isn't encryption but another way of writing – anyone who knows the table can read it. With some practice radio operators hear the letters like words.

braille.name: Braille
braille.help: The script for blind people: each character is a pattern of up to 6 dots you feel with your finger. A special sign (⠠) comes before capital letters, the number sign (⠼) before numbers – digits are then the letters A to J.
braille.crack: Braille isn't encryption either, but a script to read by touch. Conbert uses the basic letters without contractions; contracted Braille abbreviates common syllables and looks different.

crack.title: How to crack it
crack.caesarTried: All shifts tried – the most likely first:
crack.tooShort: The text is too short to guess the key word. With more than a few sentences it works.
crack.vigenereNote: The longer the secret text, the surer the guess. If a letter is off, correct it in the key word above.
crack.typeMore: Enter at least 20 letters, then Conbert tries to crack the text.
crack.keyLengthHelp: How many letters the key word has. “Automatic” guesses it from repeating letters. If that doesn't work, try the lengths one after another – with the right one the text suddenly becomes readable.
crack.longestGuess_one: The text is short: automatically Conbert only finds key words of 1 letter here. If the result is unreadable, set the length above yourself.
crack.longestGuess_other: The text is short: automatically Conbert only finds key words of up to {{count}} letters here. If the result is unreadable, set the length above yourself.

stego.cover: The picture to hide something in
stego.becomesPng: The result is saved as PNG – in a JPEG the message would get lost.
stego.alreadyHidden: This picture already holds a Conbert message. It will be replaced.
stego.what: What do you want to hide?
stego.messagePlaceholder: e.g. Meeting point: old oak, 3 pm
stego.fileToHide: The file you want to hide
stego.noPrograms: Programs and scripts (e.g. .exe, .bat, .ps1) can't be hidden – not even in a ZIP.
stego.passwordHelp: With a password the message is encrypted with AES-256 before it goes into the picture. Anyone examining the picture then only finds random data. Without a password anyone with Conbert who knows where to look can read the message.
stego.bitsHelp: How many of the lowest bits of each colour value carry the message.
stego.bitsEffect: 2 bits = twice the room. A colour value then changes by up to 3 instead of 1 – usually still invisible, but analysis tools find it more easily. 1 bit is the safe default.
stego.roomUsed: {{used}} of {{room}} room used (usually less once packed).
stego.roomTooSmall: {{used}} – the picture only offers {{room}}. Use a bigger picture or less content. Text that packs well sometimes fits anyway.
stego.done: Abracadabra – your message is now invisible in the picture! 🧙
stego.resultAlt: The picture with the hidden message
stego.keepSafe: Send the picture as a file (e.g. as a document, by e-mail or in a ZIP). WhatsApp, Instagram, Signal & co. shrink and recompress pictures – that destroys the message. Also don't save it as JPG, crop or edit it.
stego.tracesIntro: Even without a Conbert message you can check whether something unusual sits in the lowest bits.
stego.planeAlt: The lowest bits of the picture as a picture of their own
stego.planeCaption: The lowest bits as a picture: black = 0, colour = 1. Normal photos often still show outlines or smooth areas here. Even, grainy noise – often as a band from the top – hints at hidden data.
stego.chiTitle: Chi-square test from top to bottom
stego.chiAlt: Likelihood of hidden data in 5 % steps: {{values}} percent
stego.chiSuspicious: Suspicious: about the first {{percent}} % of the picture look like hidden random data.
stego.chiCalm: Inconspicuous: the test finds no trace of a message starting at the top of the picture.
stego.chiLimits: How the test works: when random bits are hidden, the values 2k and 2k+1 (e.g. 200 and 201) suddenly become almost equally common – in real photos they differ. It doesn't find very short messages or methods that scatter the bits across the whole picture. A hint, not proof.
stego.noneFound: No Conbert message found. Other programs hide things differently – you can look for traces below.
stego.lockedFound: 🔒 A message is hidden here – it is protected with a password.

errors.nothing-hidden: No Conbert message is hidden in this picture.
errors.needs-password: The message is protected with a password. Enter the password.
errors.wrong-password: The password is wrong – or the picture was changed after hiding (e.g. saved again or shrunk).
errors.damaged: The message is damaged. The picture was probably changed after hiding, e.g. shrunk by a messenger or saved as JPG.
errors.too-big: That doesn't fit into the picture. Use a bigger picture, less text or a smaller file. In expert mode, 2 bits per colour value double the room.
errors.executable: “{{name}}” is a program or script. The workshop never hides such files – so nobody can disguise malware in harmless pictures.
errors.no-picture: Conbert can't read this picture. Try a PNG, BMP or JPEG.
errors.no-audio: This isn't a sound file Conbert can read.

stego.chiUnclear: Unclear: the test fires almost everywhere. That happens with very noisy pictures (e.g. grainy photos, graphics with noise) – or when the whole picture is full of data. The test can't tell here.

invisible.coverPlaceholder: Everyone sees this, e.g. “See you tomorrow!”
invisible.passwordHelp: Without a password, anyone with a suitable tool can read the message once they know it's there. With a password it is encrypted – then you need the password to read it. The message gets a little longer.
invisible.result: Your text with the hidden message
invisible.resultInfo_one: Looks exactly like your text, but holds {{count}} more invisible character.
invisible.resultInfo_other: Looks exactly like your text, but holds {{count}} more invisible characters.
invisible.appsWarning: Copy the text with the button above, don't retype it. Some apps and websites remove invisible characters or count them towards the length limit – try it on yourself first.
invisible.inputPlaceholder: Paste a copied text here, e.g. from an email, a chat or a website.
invisible.clean: No invisible characters found – the text is clean.
invisible.conbertFound: This text holds a Conbert message. Opening it …
invisible.lockedFound: This text holds a Conbert message, protected with a password.
invisible.otherToolNote: It isn't from Conbert but probably from another program that writes bits with two invisible characters. Conbert simply read the characters as zeros and ones.
invisible.aiWarning: No person sees this text, but computers – and AI chatbots – read it too. That's how secret instructions are sometimes smuggled in. Don't pass such text to an AI without cleaning it.
invisible.markedHelp: Each coloured mark stands for invisible characters at that spot. Hover over it to see their codes.
invisible.cleanedHelp: Without invisible characters, special spaces are now normal ones. Emoji stay as they are.

zero-width.name: Zero-width characters
zero-width.help: Take up no room. They can hide messages or secretly mark a text. Normal text almost never needs them.

tag.name: Unicode tags
tag.help: Invisible copies of ordinary letters. Only meant for flag emoji – here they hide text, often instructions for AI chatbots.

variation.name: Rows of variation selectors
variation.help: A single one says how an emoji should look. Many in a row, however, can carry any data.

bidi.name: Text direction characters
bidi.help: Flip the reading direction (e.g. for Arabic or Hebrew). In English or German text they can scramble content, so file names or program code look different from what they are.

filler.name: Blank filler characters
filler.help: Look like nothing or like a space, but are letters (e.g. the Korean Hangul filler). Popular for “empty” user names.

soft-hyphen.name: Soft hyphens
soft-hyphen.help: Mark where a word may be split at the end of a line. Mostly harmless, but they can stop a search from finding the word.

space.name: Special spaces
space.help: Non-breaking, narrow or wide spaces. Mostly harmless (often copied from websites); cleaning turns them into normal spaces.

errors.nothing-hidden: There's no Conbert message hidden in this text.
errors.needs-password: The message is protected with a password. Enter the password.
errors.wrong-password: The password is wrong – or some of the invisible characters got lost when copying.
errors.damaged: The message is damaged. An app probably removed some of the invisible characters when copying or sending.

audioStego.cover: The music or recording you hide something in
audioStego.preparing: Converting to WAV … (the first time, Conbert loads its audio toolkit for this, about 30 MB)
audioStego.becomesLossless: The result is saved as FLAC or WAV – in this format the message would get lost.
audioStego.alreadyHidden: This piece already holds a Conbert message. It will be replaced.
audioStego.passwordHelp: With a password, the message is encrypted with AES-256 before it goes into the samples. Anyone examining the file then only finds noise. Without a password, anyone with Conbert who knows where to look can read the message.
audioStego.bitsHelp: How many of the lowest bits of each sample carry the message.
audioStego.bitsEffect: 2 bits = twice the room. The faint noise gets a little stronger – usually still inaudible in 16-bit music, but more likely in very quiet parts. 1 bit is the safe default.
audioStego.roomTooSmall: {{used}} – the piece only offers {{room}}. Take a longer piece or less content. Text that packs well sometimes fits anyway.
audioStego.outputHelp: FLAC is about half the size of WAV and just as lossless – the message survives in both. WAV plays in really every program.
audioStego.done: Abracadabra – your message is now inaudible in the music! 🧙
audioStego.resultAlt: The piece of music with the hidden message
audioStego.keepSafe: Send the file as it is (e.g. by email, cloud or in a ZIP). If it is saved as MP3, cut, made louder or recompressed by WhatsApp & Co. as a voice message, the message gets lost.
audioStego.noneFound: No Conbert message found. It can't survive in MP3, AAC or Ogg – only in WAV and FLAC.

errors.nothing-hidden: There's no Conbert message hidden in this piece.
errors.wrong-password: The password is wrong – or the file was changed after hiding (e.g. cut or saved again).
errors.damaged: The message is damaged. The file was probably changed after hiding, e.g. saved as MP3, cut or made louder.
errors.too-big: That doesn't fit into the piece. Take a longer piece, less text or a smaller file. In expert mode, 2 bits per sample double the room.
errors.no-audio: Conbert can't read this file as sound. Try WAV, FLAC, MP3, Ogg or M4A.

spectrogram.pictureHint: Bold outlines, writing or a logo work best. Fine details and photos tend to blur.
spectrogram.secondsHelp: How long the sound lasts. The picture is “played” from left to right over this time.
spectrogram.secondsEffect: Longer = the picture gets wider and sharper in the spectrogram, but the file gets bigger (about 86 KB per second).
spectrogram.brightnessHelp: A spectrogram shows loud parts as bright. For a dark motif on a light background (e.g. black writing on white), dark parts should therefore become loud. “Automatic” decides by the brightness of the picture.
spectrogram.rangeHelp: Between which pitches the picture lies. People hear about 20 to 16,000 Hz. A large range makes the picture taller and clearer, but very high tones sound shrill and get lost in MP3.
spectrogram.done: Abracadabra – your picture is now a sound! 🧙
spectrogram.invertedNote: Your picture is mostly light, so dark parts became loud – otherwise almost everything would be noise.
spectrogram.loud: Careful: this sounds shrill and can be loud. Turn the volume down before playing.
spectrogram.soundAlt: The sound made from your picture
spectrogram.elsewhere: View it elsewhere: open the WAV file in Audacity, click the track name and choose “Spectrogram”. The picture lies between {{min}} and {{max}} Hz. Saved as MP3, the highest tones disappear – better use WAV or FLAC then.
spectrogram.sound: The sound file you want to look at
spectrogram.howToRead: How to read it: time runs from left to right, low tones are at the bottom, high ones at the top. The brighter, the louder. Speech shows as striped patterns, music as horizontal lines, noise as an even fog.
spectrogram.finenessHelp: A spectrogram can show either time or pitch very precisely, but not both at once. “Sharper in time” shows short sounds like drum hits more clearly, “sharper in pitch” separates tones that lie close together better.

errors.noPicture: Conbert can't read this picture. Try a PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF.
errors.noAudio: Conbert can't read this file as sound. Try WAV, FLAC, MP3, Ogg or M4A.

metasecret.file: The file you hide the message in

spots.exif: The message goes into the EXIF user comment. Windows and most photo apps don't show this field.
spots.png: The message goes into the PNG's picture comment. Hardly any picture viewer shows it.
spots.gif: The message goes into the GIF's comment block. The GIF plays exactly as before.
spots.pdf: The message goes into the “Subject” field of the document properties. Only visible under File → Properties in the PDF program.
spots.quicktime: The message goes into the comment of the video or song. Picture and sound stay unchanged.
spots.audio: The message goes into the song's comment (in the ID3 tag for MP3). The sound is only copied, not converted again.

metasecret.messagePlaceholder: e.g. The key is under the flower pot
metasecret.passwordHelp: Without a password your message is plain text in the comment field – anyone who looks can read it. With a password it is encrypted with AES-256 and shows up as gibberish starting with “CNBZ1:”.
metasecret.firstTime: The first time, Conbert loads a tool for this (ExifTool about 25 MB, ffmpeg about 30 MB for music).
metasecret.done: Abracadabra – the message is now in the metadata! 🧙
metasecret.keepSafe: Send the file as a file (email, cloud, ZIP). WhatsApp, Instagram & Co. usually delete metadata. And remember: without a password, anyone looking at the properties can read the message.
metasecret.keepSafeLocked: Send the file as a file (email, cloud, ZIP). WhatsApp, Instagram & Co. usually delete metadata. Reading it takes Conbert and your password.
metasecret.reading: Reading metadata … (the first time, Conbert loads ExifTool for this, about 25 MB)
metasecret.noneFound: No text fields found – there's no message in this file's metadata.
metasecret.sealedIn: The field {{field}} holds a password-protected Conbert message.
metasecret.fieldsIntro: All fields that can hold free text – comments, descriptions, titles, keywords. People like to hide messages here, but sometimes they also hold things you'd rather not pass on.

errors.unsupported: Conbert can't write a message into this format. Possible are: {{formats}}.
errors.pdf-locked: This PDF is encrypted. Remove the password protection first, then it works.
errors.failed: The message couldn't be written. The file may be damaged or built in an unusual way. Try another file or convert it first.
errors.damaged: The message is damaged – the field was probably changed or shortened.
errors.readFailed: This file's metadata couldn't be read. It may be damaged.

fun.failed: That didn’t work with this picture. Try another one (e.g. JPG or PNG).

ascii.columnsHelp: How many characters stand side by side. More characters = more detail, but wider text. For chats 40–60 fit, for a picture 100–200.
ascii.rampHelp: Which characters are used for light and dark. “Classic” works everywhere, “Blocks” looks more solid, “Fine” shows the most shades.
ascii.coloredHelp: Every character gets the colour of its spot in the picture. Applies to the web page and the image – plain text has no colours.
ascii.darkHelp: Light characters on black, like in a terminal or dark mode. Without the tick: dark characters on white.

pixelart.widthHelp: How many big pixels side by side. Fewer = coarser and more “retro”. The Game Boy was 160 pixels wide.
pixelart.paletteHelp: The colours the picture may use – exactly those of the old devices.
pixelart.ditherHelp: Missing shades are faked with a pattern of two colours. Without dithering you get flat areas, with it fine transitions.

glitch.amountHelp: How many bytes are changed. Just a few give a clear effect; many make the picture more and more chaotic.
glitch.shiftHelp: Slides the red and blue parts apart – the typical look of a broken screen. The result is then saved as PNG.
glitch.failed: No glitch could be made from this picture. Try fewer glitches or another picture.
glitch.resultAlt: The picture with a glitch effect

deepfry.strengthHelp: How much colours, contrast and noise are exaggerated. 0 % leaves the colours as they are.
deepfry.generationsHelp: How often the picture is saved as a bad JPEG. Each time a little quality is lost – from about 50 times on it visibly falls apart.

qr.hiddenHelp: Only switch this on if your WLAN doesn’t show its name publicly. The phone then looks for it specifically.
qr.wifiWarning: The WLAN password is readable in the code. Anyone who scans it can see it – so only put it up where guests may know it.
qr.lowContrast: Too little contrast: the pattern should be clearly darker than the background. Many camera apps can’t read light patterns on a dark background.
qr.logoHelp: A small picture in the middle of the code, e.g. your company logo. The code stays readable because it can make up for errors. Conbert checks that right away.
qr.logoFailed: This picture couldn’t be loaded as a logo. Use a PNG, JPG or SVG under 10 MB.
qr.tooLong: That is too much text for a QR code. Shorten it or use a link instead.
qr.empty: Type something on the left – the code appears here.
qr.readable: Tested: the code can be read.
qr.unreadable: Conbert couldn’t read the finished code. Make the logo smaller, use more contrast or a bigger size.
qr.onlyQr: Your browser can only read QR codes. Barcodes (e.g. EAN on packaging) are recognised by Chrome on Android and Safari/Chrome on the Mac.
qr.noneFound: No code found. Tips: the code should be fully in the picture, sharp and not too small. Otherwise crop the picture to the code.
qr.urlWarning: Check the address before opening it – QR codes are used for scams, too.

favicon.fitHelp: Icons are square. “Fit” shows the whole picture (with a border top/bottom or left/right), “Fill” cuts a square out of the middle.
favicon.paddingHelp: Free space around the picture. A small border often makes logos look calmer.
favicon.fillHelp: See-through parts get this colour. The icons for iPhone and Android are always filled, because phones don’t show see-through parts.
favicon.icnsHelp: The format for programs and folders on the Mac. Web pages don’t need it.
favicon.name: Name of the app/site
favicon.nameHelp: Shown under the icon when someone adds the site to their phone’s home screen.
favicon.themeHelp: Some phones tint the address bar with it while your site is open.
favicon.previewHint: Small sizes are shown twice as big so you can see the pixels. If 16 × 16 looks too busy, a simpler picture or “Fill” often helps.
favicon.snippetHelp: Copy these lines into the <head> section of your page and put the files from the ZIP into the site’s main folder.

encode.codecHelp: Base64 is the most common (email, JSON, data URIs). “URL-safe” replaces + and / for web addresses. Hex shows every byte as two characters. URL encoding makes text fit for web addresses (a space becomes %20).
encode.binary: That is valid, but not text – rather a picture or another file. Use the “Text → file” tab.
encode.invalid: This can’t be decoded. Check that everything was copied and the right encoding is chosen.
encode.formatHelp: Base64: plain text. Data URI: Base64 with the file type in front, usable e.g. directly as . Hex: every byte as two characters.
encode.tooBig: The file is too big (at most {{max}}). As text it would be another third bigger.
encode.cut: Only the beginning is shown – copying and saving give everything.
encode.paste: Paste Base64, hex or a data URI

archiveImage.coverHint: Choose the picture that everyone will see from the outside.
archiveImage.wrongCover: Sorry, that is not a valid picture format. Please use JPG, PNG or GIF.
archiveImage.hostHint: Choose the document or picture your archive should be embedded in.
archiveImage.wrongHost: Wrong format. This trick needs a PNG or PDF.
archiveImage.what: What do you want to hide in the file?
archiveImage.files: Drag your secret files here or click to choose
archiveImage.passwordHelp: Protects your files with strong AES-256 encryption. Without this password nobody can get to the content.
archiveImage.archiveHint: Upload the ready archive you want to hide.
archiveImage.wrongArchive: This format is not supported. Please upload a ZIP, RAR or 7Z file.
archiveImage.zipHint: This trick only works with a regular ZIP archive.
archiveImage.wrongZip: That is not a valid ZIP file.
archiveImage.done: Ta-da! Your digital hiding place is ready.
archiveImage.donePdf: Mission accomplished! Your double-bottomed PDF is ready.
archiveImage.resultAlt: Preview of the finished cover file
archiveImage.howToOpen: How to open your hiding place:
archiveImage.openPicture: A double-click opens the cover picture as usual in your picture viewer.
archiveImage.openPdf: A double-click opens the document as usual in your PDF reader.
archiveImage.openZip: To get to your files, simply change the file extension to .zip (or open the file directly with a program like 7-Zip).
archiveImage.openRar: To get to your data, simply open the file with your unpacking program for {{ext}}.
archiveImage.openLocked: When unpacking, you will be asked for the password you set. Windows Explorer cannot open such ZIPs – use 7-Zip, WinRAR or the “Reveal” tab instead.
archiveImage.keepSafe: ⚠️ Important: Best send this file by email, as a direct file attachment or on a USB stick. Messengers like WhatsApp often recompress pictures – which deletes the hidden archive completely! Saving it again in a picture editor also destroys the trick.
archiveImage.revealIntro: Drop a suspicious file here to check whether it holds secrets.
archiveImage.failed: Oops, something went wrong. Please try again.

split.sizeHelp: Each part is at most this big. Pick a little less than the limit you have to meet – the last part is usually smaller.
split.presetHint: For e-mail, pick a bit less than the limit: attachments grow by about a third when sent (e.g. 18 MB for Gmail’s 25 MB).
split.tooMany: That would be more than {{max}} parts. Pick a bigger size per part.
split.fitsAlready: The file is already smaller than one part – no need to split it.
split.howToJoin: To join them: drop all parts here under “Join”, open the first part (.001) with 7-Zip, or on Windows run “copy /b file.001+file.002 file”, on Linux/macOS “cat file.0* > file”. The first time, your browser asks whether the page may save several files.

problems.notParts: These are not parts of a split file. The names must end in .001, .002 …
problems.mixed: These are parts of different files ({{names}}). Join them one by one.
problems.duplicate: Part {{number}} is there twice. Remove one of them.
problems.missing: Missing: part {{numbers}}. Drop all parts, or the file will be broken.

split.maybeMore: The last part is as big as the others. Maybe more parts follow – check that you have them all.

emojimosaic.columnsHelp: How many emojis side by side. Fewer = coarser and funnier, more = you see more detail. For chats, about 15–30 fit.
emojimosaic.setHelp: Which emojis build the picture. Coloured circles and squares match the colours best, animals and food are funnier.
emojimosaic.backgroundHelp: The colour behind the emojis in the saved picture. “See-through” leaves the gaps empty (good for using it elsewhere).
emojimosaic.resultAlt: The picture as an emoji mosaic
emojimosaic.chatHint: Tip: copy the emojis and paste them into a chat. On narrow phones a long line wraps – the fewer emojis per line, the better.

ringtone.waveform: Loudness of the song; tap to start the part there
ringtone.loadFailed: This file could not be read as sound. Try an MP3, M4A, WAV or a video with sound.
ringtone.partHelp: Which part of the song becomes the ringtone. Drag the two dots, or tap the waveform to move the part there.
ringtone.partHint: At most {{max}} seconds – iPhones take no more. 20–30 seconds are usually enough.
ringtone.fadeHelp: How long the sound swells at the start or gets quieter at the end. 0 = abrupt, 1–2 seconds sound pleasant.
ringtone.fadesTooLong: Fade in and fade out together are longer than the part – the sound never gets fully loud.
ringtone.louderHelp: Raises the volume until the loudest moment sits just below the limit. You hear the ringtone better, without distortion.
ringtone.formatHelp: Almost all phones (Android) take MP3. iPhones want M4R – that is an M4A file with another ending.
ringtone.makeFailed: The ringtone could not be made. Try again, or pick the other format.
ringtone.iphoneHint: Getting it onto the iPhone: on the computer, drag the file onto the connected iPhone in Finder (Mac) or iTunes (Windows). Without a computer: open the file in GarageBand and export it as a ringtone there.
ringtone.androidHint: Getting it onto the phone: copy the file into the “Ringtones” folder and pick it in the settings under “Sounds”.

size.title: Exact size
size.help: A file of exactly the size you want – to test upload limits, storage space and transfers.

image.title: Test picture
image.help: Colour bars, a grey ramp, a grid with a circle and a red border: you see at once whether a picture gets stretched, cropped or its colours changed.

audio.title: Test tone
audio.help: A sound to check speakers, headphones and players (WAV).

pdf.title: Test PDF
pdf.help: A PDF with big page numbers on every A4 page – handy for printers and PDF tools.

video.title: Test video
video.help: Colour bars, a running clock, the frame number and one beep per second. Your browser makes it itself.

testfiles.fillHelp: Zeros: fastest, but packs down to almost nothing. Random: like encrypted data, doesn't get smaller when packed – the most honest choice for upload tests. Text: readable numbered lines, opens in any editor.
testfiles.extHelp: Only the name changes, the content stays a test file. Use e.g. “zip” if a site only accepts certain extensions – it still won't open as a real ZIP.
testfiles.tooBig: Please enter a size between 1 byte and 4 GB.
testfiles.failed: The file couldn't be made. Maybe there isn't enough free memory – try a smaller size.
testfiles.videoFailed: Your browser couldn't make the video. Most likely it can't encode this format – try the other format (MP4/WebM) or a current Chrome, Edge or Firefox.

compare.identical: The files are identical – every byte is the same.
compare.sameSize_one: Both are {{size}}, but {{count}} byte is different (first difference at byte {{first}}).
compare.sameSize_other: Both are {{size}}, but {{count}} bytes are different (first difference at byte {{first}}).
compare.otherSize: Different sizes: A is {{a}}, B is {{b}}. First difference at byte {{first}}.
compare.tooDifferent: The texts are so different that a line-by-line view doesn't help any more (over 20,000 changed lines).
compare.resized: The pictures have different sizes. Picture B was scaled to the size of picture A for the comparison – so small differences may show up everywhere.
compare.pixelsSame: The pixels are the same (within the tolerance) – the files only differ in how they are stored, e.g. compression or metadata.
compare.pixelsChanged_one: {{percent}} % of the pixels are different ({{count}} pixel).
compare.pixelsChanged_other: {{percent}} % of the pixels are different ({{count}} pixels).
compare.sliderLabel: Dividing line between picture A (left) and picture B (right)
compare.sliderHint: Left of the line you see picture A, right of it picture B.
compare.maskLabel: Differences: changed pixels are marked red
compare.toleranceHelp: How much a pixel has to differ to count as “different” (0–128). 0 shows every little thing, even invisible noise after saving as JPEG. Higher = only clear changes.
compare.moreRanges: There are more differences – only the first 50 are listed here.

feeds.title: Profiles, channels & threads
feeds.help: Conbert looks for new content as often as you chose and downloads only that. Conbert keeps a list of what was there already – nothing is downloaded twice.
feeds.empty: No subscriptions yet. On the “Download” page, paste the link to an Instagram profile, YouTube channel or 4chan thread and choose “Save as subscription”.
feeds.intervalHelp: How often Conbert looks for something new. 4chan threads change fast (every 10 minutes is good), profiles and channels slowly. Instagram blocks accounts that look too often – there it's at most hourly.
feeds.started: Conbert is looking now – the result shows up under “Download”.
feeds.ended: Thread ended – it was archived or deleted, nothing more will come.

save.teaser: Then Conbert downloads new posts automatically as soon as they appear.
save.title: Set up a subscription
save.intro: Conbert looks regularly and downloads only what is new – even when your browser is closed.
save.name: Name (optional)
save.onlyNewOn: What's there already is skipped. Only what appears from now on is downloaded.
save.onlyNewOff_one: The first time, the newest existing post is downloaded too.
save.onlyNewOff_other: The first time, the {{count}} newest existing posts are downloaded too.
save.notifyHelp: Through the channels from the settings (e.g. to your phone). Also when a thread ends or something goes wrong.
save.sameChoices: Quality, parts, maximum per check, destination and “Afterwards automatically …” are taken from above.

overview.title: Subscriptions
overview.intro: All your subscriptions in one place: profiles, channels and threads from the downloader and tag searches on booru sites. Conbert looks regularly and downloads only what is new.
overview.addFeed: Subscribe to a profile, channel or thread
overview.addBooru: Subscribe to a booru tag search
overview.booruEmpty: No booru subscriptions yet. On the booru page you can “Save as subscription” for a search.
overview.introNoBooru: All your subscriptions in one place: profiles, channels and threads from the downloader. Conbert checks regularly and only downloads what is new.

feeds.waiting: Waiting until the running download from the same source is done – then Conbert looks.
feeds.waitingStarted: A download from the same source is running. Conbert looks as soon as it is done.

edit.limitHelp: A check loads at most this many new posts. If more arrive at once, the next check gets the rest. When new parts (e.g. reels) are added, the first check after that loads everything missing – up to 50,000.
edit.catchUpHint: Newly added parts are fetched completely at the next check – it starts right after saving.
edit.savedCatchUp: Subscription saved – Conbert is fetching the new parts now.

vault.title: My key
vault.help: A key pair like in secure messengers: with the public key anyone can encrypt files for you, but only you can open them – with your private key. The private key is made in your browser and locked with your vault password; Conbert only stores it locked and can't open it itself. The open format “age” is used.
vault.intro: Encrypt files so that only you can open them – or other users of this Conbert installation.
vault.publicKeyHelp: You can give this to anyone: it lets people encrypt files for you, but opens nothing.
vault.shareHelp: Other users of this Conbert installation can then choose you as a recipient. They only see your name and your public key.
vault.isOpen: The vault is open – you can decrypt files meant for you. It closes when you reload the page.
vault.isLocked: The vault is locked. Enter your vault password to decrypt.
vault.backupHelp: The backup is locked with your vault password. Keep it safe – with it and the password you get your key back, e.g. on a new installation. The program “age” can open it too.
vault.passwordChanged: The vault password has been changed. Old backups still open with the old password.
vault.deleteText: Files encrypted for this key can't be opened anymore afterwards – unless you have a backup. This can't be undone.
vault.passwordHelp: Not your sign-in password! Use a separate, long password, e.g. four random words. It never leaves your browser. If your sign-in password gets reset, the vault stays safe – and your files readable.
vault.warning: Nobody can reset your vault password – not even an administrator. Without the password (or a backup with its password) encrypted files stay closed forever. I understand.
vault.created: Your key is ready and the vault is open.
vault.restoreTitle: Already have a key? Load a backup
vault.restoreIntro: Choose your backup (conbert-schluessel.age) and enter its password. You can also paste an existing age key (AGE-SECRET-KEY-1…) – the password below then becomes your new vault password.
vault.restored: Your key is back and the vault is open.
vault.restoreInvalid: This is neither a Conbert backup nor an age key.

tool.for: Who should be able to open it?
tool.forHelp: Every chosen recipient can open the file with their own private key – nobody else, not even Conbert.
tool.noOwnKey: You don't have a key of your own yet.
tool.pasteKeys: More public keys (age1…), one per line
tool.passphraseHelp: Anyone who knows the password can open the file – handy for sending it to someone without a key. Share the password another way than the file (e.g. by phone). At least 10 characters.

errors.wrong-key: “{{name}}”: the file isn't encrypted for your key.

contacts.title: Contact book
contacts.intro: Save public keys under a name – when you encrypt, you just tick the recipients.
contacts.help: The contact book remembers the public keys of people you often encrypt for, with a name like “Anna”. When you encrypt (in workflows too), you tick them instead of digging out the long age1… key every time. Public keys aren't secret: they can only lock, never open. Only you can see your contact book.
contacts.name: Name
contacts.keyHelp: You get it from the person themselves, for example in a message. It starts with “age1”. In Conbert it's under Settings → My key. Never pass on a private key (AGE-SECRET-KEY-…) – it doesn't belong here.
contacts.invalidKey: That isn't a public age key. It starts with “age1” and has no spaces.
contacts.secretKey: Careful, that's a private key! Its owner keeps it to themselves. Only the public key (age1…) goes here.
contacts.added: “{{name}}” is now in your contact book.
contacts.empty: No contacts yet. Add the first one above.
contacts.deleteText: Only the entry goes. Files you already encrypted for this person still open for them. Workflows with this contact ticked won't encrypt for them any more.
contacts.myKeyHelp: Send this public key to people who want to send you encrypted files. They save it in their contact book. Passing it on is safe: only you can open.
contacts.pickEmpty: Your contact book is still empty. Add contacts in the “Contacts” tab under Workshop → Encrypt for … or in the settings.
contacts.knownAs: is in your contact book as “{{name}}”

swipe.title: Swipe
swipe.intro: Sort your downloads like on Tinder: left to delete, right to keep, up into your favourites.
swipe.help: Conbert shows you random pictures, GIFs and videos from your default storage location. Swipe a card left to delete it – Conbert remembers it existed and never downloads it again, not even through subscriptions. Swipe right to keep it; it won't come again. Swipe up and it moves into the “Favoriten” folder with the same folder structure (Instagram/KawaiiQueen/ becomes Favoriten/Instagram/KawaiiQueen/). In favourites mode, left takes a card back to its normal folder and up turns it into a premium card with a golden frame. Instead of swiping you can use the buttons or the arrow keys. You can take back your last 5 decisions – files are only deleted or moved after that. Tap a picture or video (or press F) to see it full screen and zoom in. You can keep swiping there like on the cards; the next picture follows right away. Hold X (or Shift+←) to delete every picture and video of a post (e.g. Pixiv, X, Instagram) at once. Files you deleted by hand leave the pile after the next “Sync”. The favourites mode never ends: once you have seen all favourites, they come again, freshly shuffled.
swipe.sortedHelp: Normally only cards you haven't decided on yet come up. Switched on, you also see the ones you kept – for example to clear out more later.
swipe.indexInfo: Storage location “{{target}}”: {{items}} files known, {{unsorted}} not sorted yet. Last synced: {{when}}.
swipe.neverSynced: Storage location “{{target}}” hasn't been synced yet.
swipe.emptyIndex: Conbert doesn't know any files on your storage location yet. Syncing reads all folders once – nothing is changed or copied.
swipe.cannotShow: Your browser can't show this file. You can still sort it.
swipe.legendFavorites: ← back to the normal folder · → stays a favourite · ↑ premium
swipe.undoHint_one: 1 decision is still waiting. Files are only deleted or moved once 5 newer ones follow – until then you can take it back.
swipe.undoHint_other: {{count}} decisions are still waiting. Files are only deleted or moved once 5 newer ones follow – until then you can take them back.
swipe.doneFavorites: No favourites to show right now ✨
swipe.allSortedHint: Choose other folders, switch on “Also show sorted”, or sync again when new files have arrived.

no-default.what: There is no default storage location.
no-default.cause: The swipe game shows the files of your default storage location – none is marked as default yet.

similar.title: Similar pictures
similar.intro: Finds pictures on your storage location that look the same or almost the same – even with other names, smaller or saved again. The best picture of each group is marked to keep, the others to delete.
similar.help: Conbert works out a “fingerprint” of 64 light-dark values for every picture. Copies, smaller or recompressed versions have almost the same fingerprint. Cropped or mirrored pictures are usually not found. Nothing is deleted until you click “Delete” in a group – just like swiping, and deleted pictures are never downloaded again.
similar.levelHelp: “Strict” only finds pictures that look practically the same (copies, smaller versions). “Loose” also finds burst shots and lightly edited versions – then more often something is in there you want to keep.
similar.notScanned: Nothing compared yet. Click “Compare pictures” – Conbert then looks at every picture once (with many pictures this takes a while, you may close the page).
similar.none: No similar pictures found. Try “Loose” or other folders.
similar.emptyIndex: The media index has no files yet. Load them in the “Swipe” tab with “Sync”.
similar.keepOne: At least one picture of the group has to stay.

whisper.title: Speech recognition (Whisper)
whisper.help: Whisper listens to sound and videos and writes down what is said – as subtitles (SRT, VTT) or plain text. It needs a speech model. Bigger models understand more but need more memory and time.
whisper.intro: Which speech model all users get. It is downloaded from the internet automatically on first use – or right now with “Download”.
whisper.unavailable: whisper.cpp is missing on this server. The official Docker image includes it.
whisper.notInstalled: Not downloaded yet (happens on first use)
whisper.firstUse: Source: Hugging Face (official whisper.cpp models). Every file is checked with a checksum after downloading. Stored in /data/models/whisper.

base.name: Small & fast (base)
base.help: For clear speech and weak servers. Makes more mistakes with German.

small.name: Balanced (small) – recommended
small.help: Good compromise: understands German well and runs smoothly without a graphics card.

large-v3-turbo.name: Best quality (large-v3-turbo)
large-v3-turbo.help: Also understands accents and technical terms, but needs ~2 GB of RAM and is several times slower on the CPU.

imageAi.title: Enhance
imageAi.intro: Two helpers with artificial intelligence. They run on your server – the picture is sent there for this. Afterwards it goes into the chosen format as usual.
imageAi.serverNote: The first time, the server downloads the matching AI model (once, up to ~180 MB). Big pictures need some patience without a graphics card.

background.label: Remove background
background.help: The AI finds what is in front (person, animal, product) and makes everything around it transparent – handy for stickers, product photos or collages.
background.effect: Works best with a clear subject. Fine hair or glass is sometimes nibbled a little.
background.noTransparency: {{format}} can’t store transparency – the removed background would turn white. Use PNG or WebP.

upscale.label: Upscale
upscale.help: Makes the picture bigger and invents fitting details instead of just stretching it (Real-ESRGAN). Good for small, blurry or old pictures.
upscale.effect: 2× doubles width and height, 4× quadruples them. Faces and text can look a little artificial.

settings.title: AI for pictures
settings.help: “Remove background” and “Upscale” each need an AI model on the server. They are downloaded automatically on first use – or here beforehand.
settings.intro: Models for “Enhance” in the picture card. They apply to all users.
settings.unavailable: The AI runtime (ONNX Runtime) is missing on this server. The official Docker image includes it.
settings.source: Sources: GitHub (rembg release, ISNet) and Hugging Face (Real-ESRGAN). Every file is checked with a checksum after downloading. Stored in /data/models/image.

isnet.name: Remove background (ISNet)
isnet.help: Finds the subject and separates it from the background.

realesr-general-x4v3.name: Upscale (Real-ESRGAN)
realesr-general-x4v3.help: Enlarges pictures with newly created details – small and fast.

apiTokens.intro: For scripts and automations: create a token and send it as “Authorization: Bearer …”.
apiTokens.name: What for?

admin.title: Admin overview
admin.intro: How your server is doing: load, storage, running jobs, users and engines. Updates every 5 seconds.
admin.help: Only admins see this page. Here you also decide how much space each user may take on the server. When storage is nearly full, admins get a “Storage running low” notification (if a channel is set up for it).

tiles.loadNote: {{cpus}} CPU cores – below this number all is relaxed

storage.title: Storage
storage.note: Conbert deletes uploads and results by itself after the set time. Storage locations (NAS …) don’t count here.

users.title: Storage quotas
users.help: A quota decides how much a user may have on the server at the same time: uploaded files, finished results and downloads waiting to be picked up. When it is full, Conbert takes no new files until space frees up (which happens by itself after the cleanup time). What goes to storage locations like the NAS doesn’t count.

log.title: Log
log.intro: What happened on the server – sign-ins, conversions, downloads, subscriptions, errors. You decide here how detailed it is.
log.help: The log is the server's diary. When something doesn't work, it usually says why. Passwords, keys and cookies are never written down. The log lives in the data folder under logs/ and never grows beyond the limit you set – the oldest entries go then.
log.detailHelp: The more detailed, the more entries – and the sooner the limit is reached. “Normal” is enough for every day. Switch on “Detailed” when you are tracking down a problem.

errors.label: Errors only
errors.help: Only what went wrong. Very few entries.

normal.label: Normal
normal.help: Errors, warnings and important events: sign-ins, finished conversions, downloads, subscription runs, workflows, changes to users and groups.

detailed.label: Detailed
detailed.help: Also every request to the server, every program started (ffmpeg, gallery-dl, rclone …) with its duration and error output, and every single file. Good for finding problems, but grows fast.

log.limitHelp: So the log doesn't fill your storage: when the limit is reached, the oldest entries go. Give it as a file size (MB) or as a number of lines (one line = one entry).
log.noFile: This server writes no log file.
log.clearWarning: All entries are deleted. This can't be undone.
log.empty: No entries – or none that fit your choice.
